# Novo Nordisk-Hims Patent Lawsuit Dismissed Without Prejudice


February 18, 2026


[Caleb Harris](https://www.linkedin.com/in/caleb-m-harris/)


As of August 1, 2026, the original Delaware action was closed, and public-record review found no refiling by Novo against Hims over these claims. On March 9, 2026, Novo voluntarily dismissed every claim without prejudice, and the clerk closed the case that day.


The dismissal accompanied a new commercial agreement between the companies. It did not decide whether Hims infringed Novo's semaglutide patent, whether any infringement was willful, or whether federal compounding rules affect patent liability. Novo expressly reserved the right to refile.


## Key takeaways


- Novo filed the action on February 9, 2026, alleging that compounded semaglutide products offered through Hims infringed U.S. Patent No. 8,129,343.
- Novo dismissed all claims without prejudice on March 9, before Hims served an answer or summary-judgment motion. The clerk closed the case without a merits ruling.
- Under the announced plans, Hims would add access to FDA-approved Ozempic and Wegovy, stop advertising compounded GLP-1 offerings, and retain limited access to compounded GLP-1s only for patients whose clinical needs could not be met by commercially available FDA-approved options when a provider determined a compounded product was clinically necessary.
- The complaint's direct-infringement, inducement, willfulness, damages, and compounding theories were allegations. The court did not adjudicate them.
- The action is useful as a map of a patent theory against a telehealth platform, but it did not create precedent on that theory.


## Is the Novo Nordisk-Hims patent lawsuit still active?


No. As of August 1, 2026, the original action, *Novo Nordisk A/S et al. v. Hims & Hers Health, Inc. et al.* , No. 1:26-cv-00143-CFC, was closed, and no public refiling over these claims had been identified.


Novo filed a[notice of voluntary dismissal](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.ded.91967/gov.uscourts.ded.91967.10.0.pdf) under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 41(a)(1)(A)(i) on March 9, 2026. The notice stated that Hims had not served an answer or motion for summary judgment and dismissed all claims without prejudice. The[public docket](https://dockets.justia.com/docket/delaware/dedce/1%3A2026cv00143/91967) records the notice and the case closure on the same date.


*Without prejudice* means the dismissal ended this action without permanently barring Novo from bringing the claims again. It does not mean Hims won on the merits, Novo lost on the merits, or the court rejected the patent allegations. The docket contains no decision on infringement, patent validity or enforceability, willfulness, damages, injunctive relief, or Hims' defenses. Novo's March announcement and Hims' later securities filing both say Novo retained the right to refile.


This article concerns the Delaware patent action over U.S. Patent No. 8,129,343. It does not cover separate securities, derivative, consumer, regulatory, or product-liability matters involving Hims, Novo, or GLP-1 products.


## Why did Novo Nordisk drop the Hims lawsuit, and what changed?


Novo dismissed the lawsuit on the same day the companies announced a new commercial agreement.[Novo's announcement](https://www.novonordisk.com/news-and-media/news-and-ir-materials/news-details.html?id=916512) and[Hims' announcement](https://investors.hims.com/news/news-details/2026/Hims--Hers-Announces-Strategic-Shift-for-US-Weight-Loss-Business/default.aspx) did not disclose any separate reason for the dismissal, but they identified four practical changes:


- Hims would offer access to FDA-approved Ozempic injections and Wegovy tablets and injections through its U.S. platform.
- Hims would stop advertising compounded GLP-1 offerings on its platform and in its marketing.
- Existing patients could transition to FDA-approved alternatives when a provider found that clinically appropriate.
- Hims expected to retain compounded GLP-1 access on a limited scale when a patient's needs could not be met by commercially available FDA-approved options and a provider found compounding clinically necessary.


The distinction in the last point matters. Hims did not publicly say it would stop all compounded semaglutide access. It described a narrower, provider-directed use case while shifting its marketing and broader offering toward branded products.


The public statements did not disclose a payment, damages amount, admission of infringement or noninfringement, patent-validity concession, release, exclusivity term, contract duration, or covenant never to sue. The filed dismissal was Novo's unilateral notice, not a court order approving settlement terms.


## Why did Novo sue Hims in the first place?


Novo sued because it alleged that compounded semaglutide products offered through Hims infringed claim 1 of U.S. Patent No. 8,129,343 and that Hims induced others to infringe. In 2026, the dispute moved quickly:


- **February 5:** Hims announced a compounded oral semaglutide pill with an introductory price starting at $49 for the first month of a five-month plan.
- **February 6:** The U.S. Food and Drug Administration announced planned enforcement against companies mass-marketing non-FDA-approved compounded GLP-1 products and named Hims among the companies at issue.
- **February 7:** Hims said it would stop offering access to the newly announced pill.
- **February 9:** Novo filed its patent complaint in Delaware.
- **February 26:** The court extended Hims' deadline to answer or otherwise respond to April 1.
- **March 9:** The companies announced their agreement; Novo filed the dismissal notice; and the clerk closed the case.


Novo's[complaint](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.ded.91967/gov.uscourts.ded.91967.1.0.pdf) asserted U.S. Patent No. 8,129,343, titled *Acylated GLP-1 Compounds* . The patent claims specified GLP-1 compound structures, and Novo alleged that claim 1 covered semaglutide, the active pharmaceutical ingredient in Ozempic, Wegovy, and Rybelsus.


*Semaglutide, the molecule Novo alleged was covered by claim 1 of the '343 patent.*


### Direct infringement and inducement


The complaint alleged infringement under 35 U.S.C. § 271(a) and (b). Its direct-infringement theory was that the accused compounded products contained semaglutide and fell within at least claim 1 of the '343 patent.


The[induced-infringement](https://www.tryandai.com/blog/hikma-v-amarin-induced-infringement) theory focused on Hims' role as a platform. Novo alleged that Hims knowingly induced third-party semaglutide suppliers, partner or affiliated pharmacies, affiliated medical groups, providers, and patients to engage in acts Novo characterized as direct infringement. The complaint cited Hims' instructions for using the accused products, including a video about taking compounded GLP-1 injections, as alleged encouragement.


That theory may interest patent litigators because Novo targeted the coordinating platform rather than only the entities that compounded the drugs. But the March dismissal means the theory was never tested on the merits in this case.


### Willfulness and enhanced damages


Novo also alleged willful infringement. The complaint cited the patent's Orange Book listing, statements by Hims' chief executive on an August 2024 investor call, and a demand letter Novo sent on February 8, 2026.


Novo sought enhanced damages under 35 U.S.C. § 284. Because the case ended before Hims answered, the court made no willfulness finding and awarded no damages.


### Compounding rules and patent rights


[Section 503A](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title21-section353a&num=0&edition=prelim) and[Section 503B](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title21-section353b&num=0&edition=prelim) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act conditionally exempt qualifying compounded drugs from specified federal drug requirements. They do not themselves create an exemption from the Patent Act. Novo alleged infringement, Hims did not serve an answer, and the court decided neither the patent claims nor any defense Hims might have raised based on the accused compounding activity. The FDA's February announcement addressed drug approval, quality, safety, efficacy, and marketing—not patent liability.


## What does the case mean for patent litigators?


The complaint remains a useful example of how a patent owner might plead direct and induced infringement against a platform that coordinates a distributed supply chain. It also shows how patent, regulatory, and commercial pressure can converge around the same product.


The limit is equally important: a complaint is a set of allegations, not a holding. Novo's Rule 41 notice—filed after the companies announced their commercial agreement—ended the action before the platform-inducement, willfulness, and compounding questions could mature into precedent. Any future analysis should cite the complaint for Novo's theory and the dismissal record for what the court actually did.

## Frequently asked questions


Is Novo Nordisk still suing Hims & Hers over semaglutide?


No. Novo voluntarily dismissed all claims without prejudice on March 9, 2026, and the District of Delaware closed the case that day. The court did not decide the patent allegations on the merits. Novo reserved the right to refile, but the original action remained closed as of August 1, 2026.


What does "dismissed without prejudice" mean in the Novo Nordisk-Hims case?


It means the dismissal ended this action without permanently barring Novo from bringing the claims again. It does not mean that Hims defeated the claims or that the court rejected Novo's infringement theory. Novo's dismissal notice used Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i), which permits a plaintiff to dismiss before the defendant serves an answer or summary-judgment motion.


What patent did Novo Nordisk accuse Hims of infringing?


Novo asserted U.S. Patent No. 8,129,343, titled Acylated GLP-1 Compounds. The complaint alleged that at least claim 1 covered semaglutide and that compounded semaglutide products offered through Hims infringed the patent. Because the case was dismissed, the court made no infringement or validity finding.


Did Hims stop offering compounded semaglutide?


Hims' March 9 announcement said it did not plan to end all compounded semaglutide access. It said it would stop advertising compounded GLP-1 offerings and focus on FDA-approved medicines while retaining limited compounded access for patients whose needs could not be met by commercially available approved products when a provider found compounding clinically necessary.


Did the court decide any patent defense related to compounding?


No. Sections 503A and 503B address specified federal drug requirements, not patent liability. Because Hims did not serve an answer before Novo filed its dismissal notice, the court decided neither infringement nor any patent defense. The action produced no ruling on whether the accused activities infringed the '343 patent.
